name: Exit Strategy Problem
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Getting In Is Easy. Getting Out Is the Problem.
lesson.summary: Venture investors need a realistic path to cash out through an IPO or acquisition, and quantum computing's mix of no paying customers and stretched public valuations narrows that path considerably.
lesson.body:
Venture capital is not buy and hold investing in the way a pension fund holding blue chip stocks might be. A VC fund raises money from limited partners with a promise to return it, with profit, typically within 7 to 10 years. Every investment needs a plausible exit: an IPO, where the fund sells shares on the open market over time as lockup restrictions expire, or an acquisition, where it is paid in cash or stock by a buyer. Without one of those two events, paper gains never become real returns sent back to limited partners, no matter how impressive the company's technology or its private funding valuation looks on paper.

Quantum computing narrows both paths at once. The IPO path is constrained because, as IonQ, Rigetti, and D-Wave show, quantum offerings have mostly happened through SPAC mergers rather than traditional underwritten IPOs, producing extremely volatile stocks, as covered under Market Valuation vs Revenue. A traditional IPO requires investment banks to build a credible growth and profitability story for skeptical institutional buyers, which is hard to tell for a company with No Paying Customers or revenue still in the single digit millions. The acquisition path narrows for a related reason: a corporate acquirer doing real diligence, not just reading a pitch deck, finds the same thin revenue base and asks hard questions about what, exactly, it is paying for and whether the technology is defensible.

This creates a mismatch. Private rounds have often been priced assuming eventual outcomes in the billions, consistent with the narrative multiples described earlier under Market Valuation vs Revenue. An acquirer with no interest in propping up a speculative public story values the company on more conventional grounds instead: the technology's actual capability, the team, existing contracts, and intellectual property. If a startup last raised private money at a 1 billion dollar valuation and the best acquisition offer it can generate is 150 million dollars, that is not a rounding error, it is roughly a 7 fold markdown, since 1,000 divided by 150 is about 6.7, and most investors in that late private round lose money even though the company did not fail outright in any obvious, headline grabbing way.

The exit strategy problem is a market structure problem, not just a technology problem. Even genuinely promising hardware can lack a good exit if too few buyers will pay a full price and too little revenue supports an independent public listing on fundamentals. Because so few quantum companies have paying customers in the ordinary sense, contracts for a product delivering measured value today rather than a pilot, the pool of acquirers willing to pay full price stays small.

When neither an IPO nor a full price acquisition is realistic, investors and management look for a smaller, less dignified exit instead: the acqui-hire, covered next.
